general_table_rules: Use tables to improve traceability, comparability, and scanability; avoid tables that function as marketing scorecards.
Keep a consistent column set within a table type across the report; avoid ad hoc columns that break comparability.
Use parallel phrasing across rows; each row should stand alone with label + mechanism + consequence/decision-use.
Keep cells concise; use bullets within cells for multi-part items; avoid paragraph-length cells.
Define units, scope/boundary, and time horizon conventions in headers or footnotes; do not rely on narrative to carry definitions.
Use neutral status labels (e.g., in progress; planned; not reported) and consistent placeholders for missing data.
Right-align numeric columns; left-align text columns; repeat headers on multi-page tables.
Use footnotes for technical conventions, classification references, and assurance markers; keep footnotes generic and non-identifying.
governance_tables: Use role/body mapping tables that evidence mandates, decision rights, reporting lines, artefacts, and review triggers.
Describe cadence qualitatively (regular/periodic/as required) unless specificity is required and non-identifying.
Use role-based descriptors; avoid personal identifiers and named committees unique to any entity.
Include explicit separation of ownership vs oversight vs independent assurance/review.
strategy_tables: Use a one-page strategy summary table as the organizing backbone; ensure themes/pillars are reused consistently across narrative and other tables.
Use mirrored-column tables to balance disclosure (positive vs negative impacts; risks vs opportunities).
Include standardized time-horizon fields and value-chain segment fields where relevant.
Use connectivity mapping tables to link topics to financial statement areas as navigation aids; avoid implying quantified impacts unless supported.
risk_management_tables: Use risk taxonomy/control mapping tables that link risk themes to owners, controls, assurance activities, monitoring outputs, and escalation pathways.
Maintain a consistent mini-template per risk theme within the table (risk statement → where it manifests → impacts → controls → monitoring/escalation).
Include a three-lines-of-defence roles table to clarify responsibilities and interfaces.
For analytical methods (e.g., scenario analysis), use inventory-style tables for inputs, source types, assumptions, and limitations without naming providers.
metrics_and_targets_tables: Treat the metric register as the authoritative record; narrative should explain conventions and signpost rather than duplicate content.

Ensure every metric/target includes definition, scope/boundary, reporting-period value/status, provenance (external reference and internal source/owner), mapping to report sections, and assurance indicator (if applicable).
Use consistent placeholders for missing data and include reason categories in notes.
Use reconciliation/coverage tables for scoped metrics to make inclusion/exclusion decisions transparent.
